quiz.question: What are React Fragments used for?

options.B: Grouping children without extra DOM nodes

quiz.explanation: Fragments let you group multiple children without adding extra nodes to the DOM. Instead of wrapping in a <div>, use <Fragment> or <>. This keeps the DOM cleaner, avoids styling issues from wrapper divs, and slightly improves performance. Fragments can have keys (for lists) but no other props.

quiz.question: What is the short syntax for React Fragment?

options.B: <></> empty tags

quiz.explanation: <></> is the short syntax for <React.Fragment>. It's cleaner and more concise. The downside: you can't add attributes. If you need to add a key (in lists), use the full <Fragment key={id}> syntax. The short syntax is perfect for simple grouping without needing props.

quiz.question: What is CSS specificity?

options.B: Weight determining which style rule applies

quiz.explanation: Specificity determines which CSS rule applies when multiple rules target the same element. It's calculated based on selector types: inline styles (1000), IDs (100), classes/attributes/pseudo-classes (10), elements/pseudo-elements (1). More specific selectors override less specific ones. Understanding specificity prevents !important overuse and makes CSS more maintainable.

quiz.question: Which selector has highest specificity?

options.B: Inline styles

quiz.explanation: Specificity order: (1) inline styles (highest), (2) IDs, (3) classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, (4) elements/pseudo-elements (lowest). !important overrides everything but makes CSS hard to maintain. The rule: be as specific as necessary but no more. Prefer classes over IDs for styling flexibility.

quiz.question: What is BEM methodology in CSS?

options.B: Block Element Modifier naming convention

quiz.explanation: BEM is a naming methodology: Block__Element--Modifier. Block is a component (menu), Element is part of the block (menu__item), Modifier is a variation (menu__item--active). It creates predictable, readable class names that avoid specificity issues. While verbose, it scales well and makes CSS self-documenting.

quiz.question: What is CSS-in-JS?

options.B: Writing CSS styles in JavaScript

quiz.explanation: CSS-in-JS writes styles in JavaScript (styled-components, Emotion). Benefits: scoped styles, dynamic styling based on props/state, no class name conflicts, co-location with components. Drawbacks: runtime overhead, larger bundle, no static analysis. It's popular in React for component-based styling but has trade-offs versus traditional CSS.

quiz.question: What are CSS Modules?

options.B: CSS files with locally scoped class names

quiz.explanation: CSS Modules automatically scope CSS class names to the component, preventing global conflicts. You import CSS as an object and use classes as properties: import styles from './Button.module.css'; <div className={styles.button}>. Build tools generate unique class names. You get scoping benefits without JavaScript runtime overhead.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of Flexbox?

options.B: One-dimensional layout system, flexible alignment

quiz.explanation: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system (row or column) that makes alignment, distribution, and spacing easy. It excels at: aligning items vertically, distributing space, reordering elements, and making responsive layouts. flex-grow, flex-shrink, and flex-basis control item sizing. It's perfect for navigation bars, cards, or components where you need flexible alignment.

quiz.question: How does CSS Grid differ from Flexbox?

options.B: Grid is two-dimensional, Flexbox one-dimensional

quiz.explanation: Grid is two-dimensional (rows AND columns), Flexbox is one-dimensional (row OR column). Use Grid for overall page layout, complex structures with rows and columns. Use Flexbox for component layout, aligning items in one direction. They complement each other - Grid for macro layout, Flexbox for micro layout within grid items.

quiz.question: What is REST API?

options.B: Representational State Transfer architecture style

quiz.explanation: REST is an architectural style for APIs using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources (URLs). Principles: stateless requests, resource-based URLs (/users/123), standard HTTP methods, JSON responses. RESTful APIs are predictable, scalable, and cacheable. They're the most common API style for web services.

quiz.question: What is idempotency in REST APIs?

options.B: Same request produces same result repeatedly

quiz.explanation: An idempotent operation produces the same result no matter how many times it's executed. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent (same request = same result/state). POST is not (creates new resource each time). Idempotency enables safe retries on network failures without duplicating effects, making APIs more robust.

quiz.question: How does GraphQL differ from REST?

options.B: GraphQL lets client specify exact data needed

quiz.explanation: GraphQL uses a single endpoint where clients query exactly what they need, avoiding over-fetching/under-fetching. REST uses multiple endpoints, often returning fixed data structures. GraphQL benefits: flexible queries, fewer requests, strong typing. REST benefits: simpler, better caching, familiar. Choose based on your API complexity and client needs.

quiz.question: What is memoization in programming?

options.B: Caching function results for same inputs

quiz.explanation: Memoization caches function results based on inputs. When called with the same arguments, it returns the cached result instead of recalculating. It trades memory for speed, optimizing expensive pure functions. React's useMemo and useCallback use memoization. Only memoize expensive operations - the overhead isn't worth it for cheap computations.

quiz.question: What is code splitting?

options.B: Breaking bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand

quiz.explanation: Code splitting breaks your bundle into smaller chunks loaded on-demand, reducing initial load time. Users only download code they need. Implement via dynamic imports (import()), React.lazy(), or route-based splitting. This is crucial for large apps - don't force users to download admin pages they'll never see. It significantly improves Time to Interactive.

quiz.question: What is virtual scrolling?

options.B: Rendering only visible items in long lists

quiz.explanation: Virtual scrolling (windowing) only renders items currently visible in the viewport, not the entire list. As you scroll, items are dynamically added/removed from the DOM. This makes lists of thousands/millions of items performant. Libraries like react-window and react-virtualized implement this. Essential for large datasets like table virtualization.

quiz.question: What is Mutation Observer API?

options.B: Watching DOM changes and mutations

quiz.explanation: MutationObserver asynchronously watches for DOM changes (added/removed nodes, attribute changes, text changes). It replaces deprecated mutation events with better performance. Use cases: reacting to DOM changes from third-party scripts, implementing responsive behaviors, or tracking dynamic content. It's essential when you don't control the DOM mutations directly.

quiz.question: What is ResizeObserver used for?

options.B: Detecting element size changes

quiz.explanation: ResizeObserver detects when element dimensions change, more efficient than resize events or polling. It fires when observed elements resize due to CSS, content changes, or layout shifts. Use cases: responsive components, container queries, charts that adapt to container size, or implementing custom responsive behaviors without media queries.

quiz.question: What is the 'dangerouslySetInnerHTML' prop in React?

options.B: Sets HTML content directly, bypassing sanitization

quiz.explanation: dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses React's XSS protection, directly setting HTML (like innerHTML). It's dangerous because unsanitized user input can inject malicious scripts. Only use it with trusted, sanitized content. The long name is intentionally scary to make you think twice. Prefer rendering content normally - React auto-escapes for safety.

quiz.question: Why is dangerouslySetInnerHTML dangerous?

options.B: Can expose to XSS attacks if not sanitized

quiz.explanation: It's dangerous because it can enable XSS attacks if you inject unsanitized user input. Attackers can inject <script> tags or event handlers stealing data or performing malicious actions. Always sanitize HTML (use libraries like DOMPurify) before using dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Better yet, avoid it - let React handle rendering safely.

quiz.question: What is the Virtual DOM in React?

options.B: Lightweight copy of real DOM for efficient updates

quiz.explanation: The Virtual DOM is React's lightweight representation of the actual DOM. React updates the Virtual DOM first, compares it to the previous version (diffing), calculates minimal changes needed, then applies only those changes to the real DOM (reconciliation). This batching and optimization makes React fast despite re-rendering components frequently.

quiz.question: What does the tabindex attribute do in HTML?

options.B: Controls keyboard navigation order and focusability

quiz.explanation: tabindex controls the keyboard navigation order of elements. tabindex='0' makes an element focusable in natural tab order, tabindex='-1' makes it programmatically focusable but removes it from tab order, and positive values (avoid!) set specific tab order. It's crucial for accessibility.

quiz.question: How do you prevent a specific page from being indexed by search engines?

options.A: Add noindex.txt file to page directory
options.B: Use meta tag: <meta name='robots' content='noindex'>

quiz.explanation: The <meta name='robots' content='noindex'> tag in the <head> tells search engines not to index that specific page. This is different from robots.txt which controls crawling of entire directories. You can also combine with 'nofollow': content='noindex, nofollow'.

quiz.question: When is using !important in CSS justified?

options.A: Whenever you want styles to win
options.B: Overriding third-party library styles (last resort)
options.C: In all production code for reliability
options.D: Never, it should be completely avoided

quiz.explanation: !important should be a last resort, mainly for overriding styles from third-party libraries you can't modify. Overusing it creates specificity wars and makes CSS unmaintainable. Better solutions: increase specificity, use CSS Modules, or restructure your CSS. Only use when you've exhausted other options.

quiz.question: What are CSS preprocessors like Sass/SCSS used for?

options.B: Variables, nesting, mixins before compilation to CSS

quiz.explanation: CSS preprocessors extend CSS with features like variables ($color), nesting rules, mixins (reusable style blocks), functions, and imports. They compile to standard CSS that browsers understand. While native CSS now has variables (custom properties), preprocessors still offer powerful features for organizing and maintaining large stylesheets.

quiz.question: What is the :has() pseudo-class in CSS?

options.A: Checks if element has specific class
options.B: Parent selector - styles element if it contains selector
options.C: Checks if CSS property has value

quiz.explanation: :has() is the 'parent selector' - it selects an element if it contains a matching descendant. For example, 'div:has(img)' selects divs that contain images. This was long-requested and finally added to CSS. It enables powerful conditional styling without JavaScript.

quiz.question: What are CSS container queries (@container)?

options.B: Responsive styles based on parent container size

quiz.explanation: Container queries let components respond to their parent container's size instead of viewport size. This enables truly modular responsive components - a sidebar widget can adapt differently than a main content widget, even at the same viewport size. Use 'container-type: inline-size' on parent, then '@container (min-width: 400px)' for queries.

quiz.question: What is an IIFE in JavaScript?

options.B: Immediately Invoked Function Expression

quiz.explanation: IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function that runs as soon as it's defined: (function() { /* code */ })(); or (() => { /* code */ })();. Used before ES6 modules to create private scopes, avoid polluting global namespace, and execute initialization code. Still useful for isolating code in legacy codebases.

quiz.question: What does Array.sort() do to the original array?

options.A: Returns new sorted array, original unchanged
options.B: Mutates original array in-place
options.C: Creates sorted copy and deletes original
options.D: Sorts only if you assign result

quiz.explanation: sort() mutates the original array in-place and returns the sorted array (which is the same reference). To avoid mutation, create a copy first: [...arr].sort() or use the new toSorted() method which returns a new sorted array without mutating the original.

quiz.question: How does toSorted() differ from sort()?

options.B: toSorted() returns new array, doesn't mutate

quiz.explanation: toSorted() is a new non-mutating alternative to sort(). It returns a new sorted array and leaves the original unchanged. Part of the 'change array by copy' proposal along with toReversed(), toSpliced(), and with(). Use toSorted() when you don't want to modify the original array.

quiz.question: What is Optional Chaining (?.) in JavaScript?

options.B: Safely accesses nested properties, returns undefined if null/undefined

quiz.explanation: Optional chaining (?.) safely accesses nested object properties. If any part is null/undefined, it short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing an error. Example: user?.address?.street instead of user && user.address && user.address.street. Also works with functions: obj.method?.() and arrays: arr?.[0].

quiz.question: What's the key difference between getBy, queryBy, and findBy in React Testing Library?

options.A: They select different types of elements
options.B: getBy throws error, queryBy returns null, findBy is async
options.D: getBy for production, others for testing

quiz.explanation: getBy* throws error if element not found (use for elements that should exist), queryBy* returns null if not found (use to assert non-existence), findBy* returns Promise and waits for element (use for async elements). Example: getByRole('button') throws, queryByRole('button') returns null, findByRole('button') awaits appearance.

quiz.question: What is Mock Service Worker (MSW) used for?

options.B: Intercepting and mocking API requests in tests

quiz.explanation: MSW intercepts network requests at the network level using Service Workers API. It mocks API responses in both tests and browser development without changing your app code. Define handlers once, use everywhere. More realistic than mocking fetch/axios directly since requests actually go through the network layer.

quiz.question: What is TypeScript Enum used for?

options.B: Define set of named constants

quiz.explanation: Enums define a set of named constants: enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }. By default, numeric enums start at 0. String enums require explicit values: enum Color { Red = 'RED', Blue = 'BLUE' }. They provide type safety and better readability than magic strings/numbers. However, const objects with 'as const' are often preferred for tree-shaking.

quiz.question: What's the difference between package.json and package-lock.json?

options.B: package.json has ranges, package-lock has exact versions
options.D: package.json for npm, package-lock for yarn

quiz.explanation: package.json specifies dependency version ranges (^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0). package-lock.json locks exact versions installed, including nested dependencies, ensuring deterministic installs. When you run 'npm install', it uses package-lock.json if present. Commit both files - package-lock prevents 'works on my machine' issues.

quiz.question: What problems does GraphQL solve compared to REST?

options.B: Eliminates over-fetching and under-fetching

quiz.explanation: GraphQL solves over-fetching (getting unnecessary data) and under-fetching (multiple requests for related data). With REST, /users/1 might return 20 fields when you need 3 (over-fetching), or require /users/1 then /posts?userId=1 (under-fetching). GraphQL lets clients request exactly what they need in one query, reducing bandwidth and round trips.

quiz.question: What are WebSockets primarily used for?

options.B: Real-time bidirectional communication

quiz.explanation: WebSockets provide full-duplex, bidirectional communication between client and server over a single TCP connection. Unlike HTTP (request-response), both sides can send messages anytime. Perfect for real-time features: chat, live updates, gaming, collaborative editing. After initial HTTP handshake, connection stays open for low-latency communication.

quiz.question: What is hydration in Next.js/React SSR?

options.B: Attaching JS event handlers to server-rendered HTML

quiz.explanation: Hydration is when React takes server-rendered HTML (non-interactive) and 'hydrates' it by attaching event listeners and making it interactive. Server sends plain HTML for fast initial paint, then client-side React takes over. If server and client HTML don't match, you get hydration errors. Keep rendering logic deterministic to avoid mismatches.

quiz.question: What causes hydration mismatches in Next.js?

options.B: Server and client rendering different HTML

quiz.explanation: Hydration mismatches occur when server-rendered HTML differs from client initial render. Common causes: using Date.now() (different on server/client), localStorage (not available on server), userAgent detection, random values. Solution: use useEffect for client-only code, or ensure server and client use same data/logic.

quiz.question: What does 'use client' directive do in Next.js?

options.B: Optimizes client-side performance

quiz.explanation: 'use client' marks a component and its imports as Client Components in Next.js App Router. By default, components are Server Components. Use 'use client' when you need browser APIs, hooks, event handlers, or state. Place it at the top of the file. It creates a boundary - descendants can be Server Components if they don't need client features.

quiz.question: What does JSX transform into?

options.B: React.createElement() calls

quiz.explanation:
JSX is syntactic sugar that transforms into React.createElement() calls (or the new JSX runtime).
Hello
becomes React.createElement('div', {className: 'box'}, 'Hello'). You can write React without JSX by using createElement directly, but JSX is more readable and HTML-like.

quiz.question: Why can't you use async/await directly in React component render?

options.B: Render must be synchronous; Promise isn't valid React element

quiz.explanation: React rendering must be synchronous and deterministic - it expects React elements (JSX), not Promises. An async function returns a Promise, which can't be rendered in the component tree. Use useEffect for async operations, or in React 18+ use Suspense with libraries that support it. The render function itself must return valid JSX synchronously.

quiz.question: What is react-window used for?

options.B: Virtualizing large lists by rendering only visible items

quiz.explanation: react-window (and react-virtualized) implements virtualization/windowing - rendering only the visible portion of a large list. Instead of rendering 10,000 items (slow), it renders ~20 visible items plus a small buffer. As you scroll, items are dynamically added/removed. Essential for performance with large datasets.

quiz.question: What are the benefits of React Query over manual useEffect data fetching?

options.B: Automatic caching, loading states, refetching, error handling

quiz.explanation: React Query provides automatic caching, background refetching, loading/error states, request deduplication, pagination, infinite scroll, optimistic updates, and more - all out of the box. Manual useEffect requires managing all this yourself. It treats server state as a cache, not component state, which is the correct mental model.

quiz.question: What are optimistic UI updates?

options.B: Updating UI immediately before server confirmation

quiz.explanation: Optimistic updates immediately update the UI assuming the server request will succeed, then rollback if it fails. Example: clicking 'like' instantly shows liked state before API responds. This makes apps feel faster and more responsive. Implement with React Query's onMutate/onError, or manually save previous state for rollback.

quiz.question: What is Redux-Saga used for?

options.B: Managing side effects in Redux with generator functions

quiz.explanation: Redux-Saga handles side effects (API calls, async operations) in Redux using generator functions (function*). Sagas listen for actions, perform async work, and dispatch new actions. Benefits: testable without mocking, cancellable, sequential/parallel control with yield. Alternative to Redux Thunk. Uses ES6 generators for more powerful async flow control.

quiz.question: What are generator functions in JavaScript?

options.B: Functions that can pause/resume with yield

quiz.explanation: Generator functions (function*) can pause execution with yield and resume later. Calling a generator returns an iterator. Use .next() to resume execution until the next yield. They enable lazy evaluation, custom iterators, and powerful async patterns (used by Redux-Saga). Example: function* gen() { yield 1; yield 2; }

quiz.question: What is Lighthouse used for?

options.B: Auditing web page performance, accessibility, SEO

quiz.explanation: Lighthouse is Google's open-source tool for auditing web pages. It measures performance (Core Web Vitals), accessibility, SEO, best practices, and PWA readiness. Generates scores and actionable recommendations. Available in Chrome DevTools, CLI, or as a library. Essential for optimizing user experience and search rankings.

quiz.question: What is First Contentful Paint (FCP)?

options.B: Time when first content renders on screen

quiz.explanation: FCP measures when the browser first renders any text, image, or canvas. It indicates when the user sees something happening, even if it's not useful content yet. Good FCP is under 1.8s. Different from LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) which measures the largest element. FCP is part of Core Web Vitals for measuring perceived load speed.

quiz.question: What is ARIA in web accessibility?

options.B: Array Interface Accessibility

quiz.explanation: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) adds semantic information to HTML for assistive technologies. Attributes like role='button', aria-label='Close', aria-expanded='true' help screen readers understand interactive components. Use semantic HTML first (button, nav, etc.), ARIA when HTML isn't enough. Remember: first rule of ARIA is don't use ARIA if HTML works.

quiz.question: How do Styled Components differ from CSS Modules?

options.B: Styled: CSS-in-JS runtime; Modules: scoped CSS files
options.C: Styled for React, Modules for Vue

quiz.explanation: Styled Components is CSS-in-JS - styles in JavaScript with runtime generation, dynamic styling from props, no class name conflicts. CSS Modules are regular CSS files with locally-scoped class names, compiled at build time, no runtime cost. Trade-offs: Styled Components are more powerful/flexible but have runtime overhead; CSS Modules are faster but less dynamic.

quiz.question: What is TTFB (Time to First Byte)?

options.A: Time from when the browser starts parsing HTML until the first pixel renders on screen
options.B: Time from request until first byte of response arrives
options.C: Time for JavaScript bundle to download and execute, making the page interactive
options.D: Time for largest content element to render (same as LCP metric)

quiz.explanation: TTFB measures the time from when a user makes an HTTP request until the first byte of the response reaches their browser. It includes DNS lookup, connection time, and server processing. Good TTFB is under 600ms. It's different from FCP (when content renders) - TTFB is purely about network and server response time.

quiz.question: Which rendering strategy typically has the BEST (lowest) TTFB?

options.A: SSR because server-rendered HTML is optimized for speed and caching
options.B: CSR because the initial HTML shell is minimal and served instantly
options.D: All have identical TTFB when properly configured with CDN

quiz.explanation: SSG has the best TTFB because pre-built HTML files are served directly from a CDN with no server processing needed. SSR has slower TTFB since the server must generate HTML for each request. CSR has fast TTFB for the initial HTML shell, but that HTML is nearly empty. ISR combines both - cached pages have SSG-like TTFB, while regenerating pages have SSR-like delays.

quiz.question: What's the relationship between TTFB and FCP?

options.A: TTFB always happens after FCP because the server needs rendered content first
options.B: TTFB always happens before FCP
options.C: TTFB and FCP measure the same metric with different names (legacy vs modern)
options.D: They measure completely unrelated aspects - TTFB is server-side, FCP is client-side

quiz.explanation: TTFB (Time to First Byte) always occurs before FCP (First Contentful Paint). TTFB measures when the server response starts arriving, while FCP measures when the browser actually renders the first content. The time between TTFB and FCP includes downloading the rest of the HTML, parsing it, downloading CSS/JS, and rendering. For SSG, this gap is small; for CSR, it's larger.

quiz.question: Which approach does NOT improve TTFB?

options.A: Using a CDN to serve static files from edge locations closer to users
options.B: Code splitting your JavaScript bundle
options.C: Optimizing database queries and adding indexes to reduce server processing time
options.D: Implementing Redis caching to avoid redundant database calls on each request

quiz.explanation: Code splitting improves load time and FCP by reducing the amount of JavaScript to download, but doesn't affect TTFB. TTFB only measures time until the FIRST byte arrives - it's about network and server speed, not bundle size. To improve TTFB: use CDN, optimize server code, cache responses, use HTTP/2, reduce DNS lookup time, or switch from SSR to SSG.

quiz.question: Why does CSR typically have fast TTFB but slow FCP?

options.A: Server must generate complex HTML slowly, but once received it displays immediately
options.B: Initial HTML is minimal, but browser must download and execute JS to render content
options.C: CSR requires multiple server round trips to authenticate and fetch user-specific data
options.D: CDN can't cache client-rendered pages effectively, causing delays in content delivery

quiz.explanation: CSR sends a nearly empty HTML shell quickly (fast TTFB), but the page remains blank until JavaScript downloads, parses, and executes to render content (slow FCP). The browser must fetch data via API calls, process it, and then render - all client-side. This creates a "loading spinner" experience. SSR/SSG avoid this by sending ready-to-display HTML.

quiz.question: When is CSR (Client-Side Rendering) the BEST choice?

options.A: Public marketing pages that need excellent SEO for organic search traffic
options.B: Admin dashboards behind authentication with frequent data updates
options.C: Blog posts and documentation sites with mostly static, SEO-critical content
options.D: E-commerce product pages that need to rank well in Google Shopping results

quiz.explanation: CSR excels for authenticated apps where SEO doesn't matter and data changes frequently. Admin dashboards, internal tools, and apps like Gmail benefit from CSR's simplicity - no server rendering complexity, easy to deploy to static hosting, and interactive once loaded. For public pages needing SEO, SSR/SSG are better choices.

quiz.question: Where does the actual HTML generation happen in CSR?

options.A: On the server during build time, then cached for instant delivery
options.B: On the server for each request, ensuring fresh data on every page load
options.C: In the user's browser using JavaScript
options.D: On a CDN edge server using edge computing to reduce latency

quiz.explanation: In CSR, the server sends minimal HTML with a JavaScript bundle. The user's browser downloads and executes this JavaScript, which then generates the HTML (DOM elements), fetches data from APIs, and renders the UI. Everything happens client-side. This is why CSR apps show a blank page or loading spinner initially - the browser is doing all the work.

quiz.question: What's the TTFB vs FCP tradeoff with SSR?

options.A: Slower TTFB (server processing), but faster FCP (HTML ready to display)
options.B: Faster TTFB and faster FCP than all other methods, making it the best choice
options.C: Slower TTFB and slower FCP than CSR because of server round-trip overhead
options.D: TTFB and FCP are identical in SSR since rendering and delivery happen simultaneously

quiz.explanation: SSR has slower TTFB because the server must process the request, fetch data, and generate complete HTML before responding. However, once that HTML arrives, FCP is fast - the browser can immediately display content. Compare to CSR: fast TTFB (empty HTML shell), slow FCP (must download/execute JS). SSR prioritizes getting visible content to users quickly, even if first byte takes longer.

quiz.question: Why does SSR typically cost more to run than SSG?

options.A: SSR requires more expensive programming languages like Java instead of JavaScript
options.B: SSR needs server resources for EVERY request; SSG pre-builds and serves static files
options.C: SSR can't use CDN caching effectively, requiring expensive origin servers for all traffic
options.D: SSR requires specialized database software licenses and high-performance infrastructure

quiz.explanation: SSR generates HTML on-demand for each request, requiring constant server compute resources (CPU, memory). SSG builds pages once at build time and serves them as static files from cheap CDN storage - no server needed per request. For high-traffic sites, SSR means paying for servers to handle millions of render operations, while SSG pays pennies for CDN bandwidth.

quiz.question: What's SSR's main advantage over SSG for dynamic content?

options.A: SSR is significantly faster than SSG for all use cases due to optimized rendering
options.B: SSR fetches latest data on every request; SSG shows stale data until rebuild
options.C: SSR has better SEO than SSG because search engines prefer dynamically rendered pages
options.D: SSR works offline using service workers; SSG requires constant internet connection

quiz.explanation: SSR's killer feature is data freshness - every request fetches current data from the database and generates updated HTML. SSG shows whatever data existed at build time until you rebuild. For rapidly changing content (live sports scores, stock prices, user-specific data), SSR ensures users always see the latest. ISR bridges this gap with periodic regeneration.

quiz.question: Why does SSG provide the best TTFB AND FCP?

options.A: SSG uses special browser APIs like Service Workers for instant loading
options.B: Pre-built HTML served from CDN = instant TTFB, complete HTML = instant FCP
options.C: SSG compresses files better than other methods using advanced algorithms
options.D: SSG only works with small websites, making optimization easier than large apps

quiz.explanation: SSG pre-generates all HTML at build time and serves it from a CDN. TTFB is minimal - just the time to get a file from the nearest CDN server (often <100ms). FCP is also fast because the HTML is complete and ready to display. No server processing (unlike SSR), no waiting for JavaScript execution (unlike CSR). The tradeoff is stale data - you need to rebuild to update content.

quiz.question: What's a limitation of SSG for large websites?

options.A: SSG can't handle more than 100 pages due to browser caching limitations
options.B: Build time grows with page count - 10,000 pages might take hours to rebuild
options.C: SSG files are too large for CDN storage, requiring expensive origin servers
options.D: SSG doesn't work with modern frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, or Astro

quiz.explanation: SSG must generate every page at build time. A blog with 10 posts builds in seconds, but an e-commerce site with 100,000 products could take hours. Any content change requires a full rebuild. This is why large sites use ISR (incremental updates) or hybrid approaches (SSG for marketing pages, SSR for product pages). Build-time scales linearly with page count.

quiz.question: How does ISR's TTFB behave when a page needs regeneration?

options.A: Always instant like SSG regardless of revalidation status
options.B: First user after revalidation gets slower TTFB (SSR-like), subsequent users get fast cached version
options.C: Always slow like SSR because every request triggers server-side processing
options.D: TTFB is random and unpredictable depending on server load

quiz.explanation: ISR serves cached (static) pages with SSG-like TTFB most of the time. After the revalidation period expires, the next user still gets the stale cached version quickly (good UX), but triggers background regeneration. Once regeneration completes, future users get the updated cached version. This "stale-while-revalidate" pattern gives you SSG speed with SSR freshness.

quiz.question: What's ISR's advantage over SSG for frequently updated content?

options.A: ISR is significantly faster than SSG at rendering pages due to optimized algorithms
options.B: ISR updates individual pages without rebuilding entire site
options.C: ISR has better SEO than SSG because Google rewards frequently regenerated content
options.D: ISR works offline using service workers while SSG requires constant connectivity

quiz.explanation: SSG requires rebuilding the entire site to update any page - impractical for frequent updates. ISR lets you set a revalidation time (e.g., 60 seconds) per page. After that time, the page regenerates in the background when requested, without touching other pages. Update a product price every minute without rebuilding 100,000 pages. Best of both worlds: SSG speed + fresh content.

quiz.question: Which statement about ISR is TRUE?

options.A: ISR is a standard web feature available in all modern frameworks and browsers
options.B: ISR is primarily a Next.js feature, not available in vanilla React
options.C: ISR requires special CDN support like Cloudflare or Fastly with edge computing
options.D: ISR only works with serverless functions like AWS Lambda or Vercel Functions

quiz.explanation: ISR is a Next.js-specific feature introduced in Next.js 9.5. Vanilla React doesn't have ISR - you'd need to build similar functionality yourself. Other frameworks like Remix, Astro, or Gatsby have their own approaches to incremental updates, but ISR with revalidation periods is Next.js's innovation. It requires server-side capability to regenerate pages on-demand.

quiz.question: What are the three WCAG conformance levels?

options.B: A (minimum), AA (mid-range), AAA (highest)

quiz.explanation: WCAG defines three conformance levels: A (minimum), AA (mid-range, most common legal requirement), and AAA (highest, hardest to achieve). Most organizations aim for AA compliance. Level A covers basic accessibility, AA addresses major barriers, AAA is the gold standard but often impractical for all content.

quiz.question: What's the minimum color contrast ratio for normal text under WCAG AA?

options.B: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text
options.C: 7:1 for normal text, 4.5:1 for large text
options.D: 2:1 for normal text, no requirement for large text

quiz.explanation: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text (under 18pt or 14pt bold) and 3:1 for large text. AAA is stricter: 7:1 for normal, 4.5:1 for large. This ensures text is readable for people with visual impairments. Use tools like WebAIM's contrast checker to verify your colors meet these requirements.

quiz.question: Which WCAG principle requires all functionality be keyboard accessible?

options.B: Operable - users must operate the interface
options.C: Understandable - users must understand the information
options.D: Robust - content works with assistive technologies

quiz.explanation: WCAG has 4 principles (POUR): Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. "Operable" requires all functionality be available from keyboard, no keyboard traps, and sufficient time to interact. Many users can't use a mouse due to motor disabilities, so keyboard access is critical for accessibility.

quiz.question: When should an image have an empty alt attribute (alt="")?

options.A: Never - all images need descriptive alt text for screen readers
options.B: When the image is decorative or its meaning is conveyed in surrounding text
options.C: Only for images smaller than 100x100 pixels
options.D: When the image is loaded from external CDN sources

quiz.explanation: Use alt="" for decorative images (borders, spacers) or when the image meaning is already in text nearby. This tells screen readers to skip it, avoiding redundant announcements. Informative images need descriptive alt text. Missing alt entirely (no attribute) causes screen readers to announce the filename, which is worse than alt="".

quiz.question: Why is removing CSS focus outlines (outline: none) problematic for accessibility?

options.A: It causes browser performance issues and slower page rendering
options.B: Keyboard users can't see which element is focused, breaking navigation
options.C: Screen readers can't detect focused elements without visual outlines
options.D: It's actually fine - focus outlines are optional for accessibility

quiz.explanation: Focus indicators (outline) show keyboard users where they are on the page. Removing them with outline: none makes navigation impossible for keyboard-only users. If you don't like the default outline, replace it with a custom one (outline: 2px solid blue), never just remove it. This is a WCAG Level A requirement.

quiz.question: Why is semantic HTML important for accessibility?

options.A: It makes the website load faster by reducing JavaScript dependencies
options.B: Screen readers rely on semantic tags to understand page structure and navigation
options.C: Semantic HTML is only important for SEO, not accessibility
options.D: It prevents XSS attacks by validating user input automatically

quiz.explanation: Semantic HTML (header, nav, main, article, button) provides meaning to assistive technologies. Screen readers use these tags to build a page outline, jump between sections, and understand interactive elements. A div with onClick isn't announced as clickable, but a button element is. Always use the right tag for the job.

quiz.question: When should you use aria-label vs aria-labelledby?

options.A: aria-label for visible labels, aria-labelledby for hidden labels
options.B: aria-label adds custom text; aria-labelledby references existing element's text
options.C: They're identical - use whichever you prefer for consistency
options.D: aria-label for buttons, aria-labelledby for form inputs only

quiz.explanation: aria-label directly provides label text (aria-label="Close menu"), while aria-labelledby references another element's ID (aria-labelledby="dialog-title"). Use aria-labelledby when the label text already exists on screen. Use aria-label when you need to add accessible text that isn't visible. Prefer visible labels when possible.

quiz.question: What is a "skip to main content" link and why is it important?

options.A: A hidden link that skips loading images for faster page performance
options.B: A link (usually first in tab order) that lets keyboard users bypass navigation
options.C: An SEO technique to help search engines find primary content faster
options.D: A debugging tool that skips CSS loading during development

quiz.explanation:
Skip links let keyboard users jump directly to main content, bypassing repetitive navigation. Without it, users must tab through dozens of nav links on every page. It's often visually hidden but appears on focus. This is a WCAG Level A requirement. Implementation: Skip to main content at the top, with
around your content.

quiz.question: Which is a common screen reader used for accessibility testing?

options.A: Chrome DevTools Lighthouse only covers all screen reader testing needs
options.B: NVDA (Windows), JAWS (Windows), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS)
options.C: Automated tools like axe-core eliminate the need for manual testing
options.D: Screen reader testing is optional if you use semantic HTML

quiz.explanation: Real screen reader testing is essential. Popular screen readers: NVDA (free, Windows), JAWS (paid, Windows), VoiceOver (free, macOS/iOS), TalkBack (Android). Automated tools catch ~30% of issues; manual testing finds the rest. Test your site with at least one screen reader to understand the actual user experience.

quiz.question: What's the correct way to associate a label with an input for accessibility?

options.A: Place label text in placeholder attribute: <input placeholder="Email">
options.B: Use <label for="email">Email</label> with <input id="email">
options.C: Put label text in aria-label: <input aria-label="Email">

quiz.explanation: Proper label association uses for/id matching: <label for="email">Email</label><input id="email">. This lets screen readers announce the label, increases click area (clicking label focuses input), and is WCAG Level A. Placeholders disappear when typing and aren't replacements for labels. Aria-label works but visible labels are better.

quiz.question: What does WCAG Success Criterion 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) require?

options.A: All focusable elements must have visible focus indicators when focused
options.B: All images must be visible and not hidden with CSS display: none
options.C: Focus must automatically move to error messages when forms fail
options.D: All text must be visible without requiring horizontal scrolling

quiz.explanation: SC 2.4.7 (Level AA) requires a visible focus indicator when any UI component receives keyboard focus. This is critical for keyboard navigation - users need to see where they are. Default browser outlines satisfy this, but custom focus styles must be clearly visible. Don't just remove focus indicators.

quiz.question: What is aria-live used for in accessibility?

options.A: To indicate elements that are currently visible on screen vs hidden
options.B: To announce dynamic content changes to screen readers without moving focus
options.C: To mark elements that update in real-time via WebSocket connections
options.D: To improve performance by lazy-loading content only when visible

quiz.explanation:
aria-live creates "live regions" that announce dynamic changes to screen readers. Values: polite (wait for pause), assertive (interrupt immediately), off (default). Use for status messages, alerts, or dynamic content updates. Example:
5 items added to cart
. Without it, screen reader users miss dynamic updates.

quiz.question: What's the main difference between Next.js App Router and Pages Router?

options.A: App Router uses app/ directory with React Server Components by default
options.B: Pages Router is faster and recommended for production applications
options.C: App Router only works with TypeScript, Pages Router supports both JS and TS
options.D: They're identical features - just different naming conventions for the same routing

quiz.explanation: App Router (Next.js 13+) uses the app/ directory and React Server Components by default, enabling better performance and new patterns. Pages Router uses pages/ directory with traditional React components. App Router is the future but Pages Router is still fully supported. Both can coexist in the same project.

quiz.question: What's the default behavior of components in Next.js App Router?

options.A: All components are Client Components by default, add 'use server' for server rendering
options.B: All components are Server Components by default, requiring 'use client' for client
options.C: Next.js automatically detects based on hooks usage and browser API calls
options.D: Components run universally on both server and client (isomorphic rendering)

quiz.explanation: In App Router, all components are Server Components by default. They run only on the server, can't use hooks/browser APIs, but can directly access databases. Add 'use client' at the top to make a component a Client Component (for interactivity, hooks, browser APIs). This shift improves performance by reducing client JS.

quiz.question: How do you fetch data in Next.js Server Components?

options.A: Use useEffect with fetch API like traditional React components
options.B: Use async/await directly in the component function
options.C: Only getServerSideProps and getStaticProps methods are supported
options.D: Data fetching requires separate API routes in app/api directory

quiz.explanation:
Server Components can be async functions! Just use async/await directly: async function Page() { const data = await fetch(...); return
{data}
}. No useEffect, no special functions. This is simpler than getServerSideProps. Client Components can't be async - they still need useEffect or libraries like SWR/React Query.

quiz.question: In Next.js App Router, what file creates a route?

options.A: Any .tsx/.jsx file in the app/ directory becomes a route automatically
options.B: Only page.tsx/page.jsx files create accessible routes
options.C: Files named index.tsx are required for every route in the application
options.D: Routes must be registered manually in app/routes.config.js configuration

quiz.explanation: Only page.tsx (or page.jsx) files create routes. Other files like layout.tsx, loading.tsx, error.tsx have special meanings but don't create routes. This lets you colocate components/utilities in the same folder. Example: app/blog/page.tsx → /blog route, but app/blog/PostCard.tsx isn't a route.

quiz.question: What's special about layout.tsx in Next.js App Router?

options.A: It wraps pages in that folder and nested folders, persisting between navigations
options.B: It's just a regular component file with no special framework behavior
options.C: It only applies to the immediate page.tsx in the exact same folder
options.D: It replaces page.tsx completely and becomes the main route component

quiz.explanation: layout.tsx wraps pages in that folder and all nested folders, creating a UI shell that persists during navigation. Layout state is preserved when navigating between pages, avoiding re-renders. Perfect for nav bars, sidebars. Root layout.tsx is required and wraps the entire app. Layouts can't use useState (Server Components) but nested Client Component layouts can.

quiz.question: How do you show loading UI in Next.js App Router?

options.A: Use useEffect with loading state variable in each component manually
options.B: Create loading.tsx file - automatically shown while page loads
options.C: Configure loading behavior in getServerSideProps with loading prop
options.D: Loading states require custom Suspense boundaries in every component

quiz.explanation: Create loading.tsx next to page.tsx - Next.js automatically shows it while the page loads, then swaps to the page when ready. Built on React Suspense. You can have loading.tsx at any level - it applies to that page and nested pages. Simple pattern: loading.tsx shows spinner, page.tsx fetches data async.

quiz.question: How does error.tsx work in Next.js App Router?

options.A: It's a global 404 page for all missing routes in the application
options.B: It's an Error Boundary that catches errors in that route segment
options.C: It only catches build-time TypeScript errors, not runtime failures
options.D: It's deprecated in App Router - use try/catch in page.tsx instead

quiz.explanation: error.tsx is an Error Boundary that catches runtime errors in the route segment (page and children). It must be a Client Component ('use client') and receives error and reset props. It doesn't catch errors in layout.tsx in the same folder (use parent's error.tsx). For root layout errors, use global-error.tsx.

quiz.question: How do you create API endpoints in Next.js App Router?

options.A: Create files in pages/api/ directory using the legacy Pages Router pattern
options.B: Create route.ts files with exported HTTP method functions (GET, POST, etc.)
options.C: Define all API endpoints centrally in api.config.ts at project root
options.D: API routes aren't supported - App Router is for UI rendering only

quiz.explanation: Create route.ts (or route.js) in app/ directory and export functions named GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc. Example: app/api/users/route.ts with export async function GET() { return Response.json({users: []}) }. These replace pages/api routes. They run on the server and can access databases directly.

quiz.question: How do you create a dynamic route like /blog/[slug] in App Router?

options.A: Create app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx - slug available in params prop
options.B: Use URL query strings: app/blog/page.tsx?slug=post-title pattern
options.C: Create app/blog/:slug/page.tsx using Express-style colon syntax
options.D: Dynamic routes require manual configuration in next.config.js routes

quiz.explanation: Use [folderName] for dynamic segments: app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx. The slug is available in params: async function Page({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }). Catch-all routes use [...slug], optional catch-all use [[...slug]]. This file-based routing is Next.js's killer feature.

quiz.question: How do you set page metadata (title, description) in App Router?

options.A: Use <Head> component from next/head like in Pages Router pattern
options.B: Export a metadata object or generateMetadata function from page.tsx
options.C: Configure all metadata centrally in next.config.js for entire site
options.D: Install and configure react-helmet library for metadata management

quiz.explanation: Export metadata object: export const metadata = { title: 'Home', description: '...' } or use generateMetadata function for dynamic metadata: export async function generateMetadata({ params }) { return { title: params.slug } }. This is type-safe and works with Server Components. next/head is for Pages Router.

quiz.question: What can Next.js middleware do?

options.A: Run code before requests - auth checks, redirects, rewrites, headers
options.B: Only handle server-side logging and analytics tracking functionality
options.C: Replace all API routes with single centralized middleware function
options.D: Middleware is deprecated - use Route Handlers or Server Actions instead

quiz.explanation: Middleware runs before every request in middleware.ts at project root. Use it for: authentication checks, redirects, setting headers, rewriting URLs, A/B testing. It runs on Edge Runtime (fast, globally distributed). Example: check auth token, redirect to /login if missing. Runs before pages/routes/static files.

quiz.question: When does Next.js use Static Rendering vs Dynamic Rendering in App Router?

options.A: All routes are dynamic - static requires export const dynamic = 'force-static'
options.B: Routes are static by default, become dynamic if using cookies, headers, searchParams
options.C: You must manually configure rendering mode in next.config.js for each route
options.D: App Router only supports dynamic rendering - static was removed completely

quiz.explanation: Next.js tries static rendering by default (build-time). Routes become dynamic if you use: cookies(), headers(), searchParams, or uncached data fetching. You can force: export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' (always SSR) or 'force-static' (always SSG). This automatic detection is smarter than Pages Router's getServerSideProps/getStaticProps.

quiz.question: What are Parallel Routes in Next.js App Router?

options.A: Loading multiple pages simultaneously in different browser tabs for better UX
options.B: Rendering multiple route segments in same layout using @folder slots
options.C: Performance optimization that preloads all routes on initial page load
options.D: Running multiple API routes in parallel for faster data fetching operations

quiz.explanation:
Parallel Routes let you render multiple pages in the same layout using slots. Create @folderName folders, reference in layout: function Layout({ children, @analytics, @team }) { return
{children}{analytics}{team}
}. Useful for dashboards with multiple sections, modals, or conditional rendering. Advanced feature for complex UIs.

quiz.question: What do Intercepting Routes (.) in Next.js allow?

options.A: Show route in modal on navigation, but full page on direct visit/refresh
options.B: Intercept and modify API calls to add authentication or logging
options.C: Block users from accessing routes based on permission levels
options.D: Automatically redirect unauthenticated users to login page

quiz.explanation: Intercepting Routes use (.) convention to show a route in a modal when navigating from within the app, but load full page on direct visit/refresh. Example: show photo in modal when clicking from feed, but full page when sharing URL. Patterns: (.) same level, (..) parent, (...) root. Great for modals, overlays.

quiz.question: What are Server Actions in Next.js?

options.A: Functions marked 'use server' that run on server, callable from Client Components
options.B: Deprecated API pattern - replaced entirely by Route Handlers in App Router
options.C: Server-side analytics and performance tracking functionality only
options.D: Automatic optimizations that improve server response times globally

quiz.explanation: Server Actions are async functions with 'use server' at the top, running on the server but callable from Client Components. Perfect for mutations (form submissions, database updates) without API routes. Example: async function createUser(formData) { 'use server'; await db.insert(...) }. Use in forms with action prop. Simpler than Route Handlers for mutations.

quiz.question: What's the main difference between git rebase and git merge?

options.A: Rebase is faster than merge for large repositories with many commits
options.B: Rebase rewrites history by moving commits; merge creates a merge commit
options.C: Merge is deprecated - modern Git workflows only use rebase
options.D: They're identical - just different commands for the same operation

quiz.explanation: Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history with new commit SHAs. Merge combines branches with a merge commit, preserving original history. Rebase creates linear history (cleaner), merge preserves complete history (safer). Never rebase commits that have been pushed to shared branches - it breaks collaboration.

quiz.question: You need to switch branches but have unfinished, uncommitted work. What does running git stash do with it?

options.A: Permanently deletes uncommitted changes to clean working directory
options.B: Temporarily saves uncommitted changes for later reapplication
options.C: Creates a new branch from uncommitted changes automatically
options.D: Commits changes to a special stash branch in remote repository

quiz.explanation: git stash temporarily saves uncommitted changes (both staged and unstaged), reverting to a clean working directory. Use git stash pop to reapply changes, or git stash list to see all stashes. Useful when switching branches without committing incomplete work. Changes aren't lost - they're stored in stash stack.

quiz.question: What does git cherry-pick do?

options.A: Selects specific files to commit from working directory changes
options.B: Applies a specific commit from one branch to another branch
options.C: Deletes specific commits from branch history permanently
options.D: Automatically picks the best commit for merging conflicts

quiz.explanation: git cherry-pick <commit-sha> applies changes from a specific commit to your current branch, creating a new commit. Useful for pulling single bug fixes from one branch to another without merging everything. The new commit has different SHA (not the same commit). Use carefully - can create duplicate commits across branches.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between git reset and git revert?

options.A: Reset moves HEAD backward; revert creates new commit undoing changes
options.B: Reset is safer for shared branches; revert rewrites public history
options.C: Revert is faster for large codebases with extensive change history
options.D: They're identical - both undo commits using the same mechanism

quiz.explanation: git reset moves HEAD to a previous commit, erasing commits from history (dangerous for pushed commits). git revert creates a NEW commit that undoes changes, preserving history (safe for pushed commits). Reset is for local-only changes, revert is for shared branches. Reset options: --soft (keep changes staged), --mixed (unstage), --hard (delete changes).

quiz.question: What is Git Flow branching strategy?

options.A: Single main branch - all commits go directly to main/master
options.B: Main, develop, feature/, release/, hotfix/ branches with strict workflow
options.C: Trunk-based development with short-lived feature flags only
options.D: Each developer has their own permanent branch forever

quiz.explanation: Git Flow uses: main (production), develop (integration), feature/* (new features), release/* (release prep), hotfix/* (urgent fixes). Features branch from develop, merge back after review. Releases branch from develop, merge to main and develop. Good for scheduled releases but complex. Alternative: trunk-based (simpler, frequent merges to main).

quiz.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict in Git?

options.A: Git automatically resolves conflicts - no manual intervention needed
options.B: Manually edit conflicted files, remove markers, stage and commit
options.C: Use git merge --force to overwrite conflicting changes automatically
options.D: Delete the branch and recreate it to avoid conflict resolution

quiz.explanation: When conflicts occur, Git marks files with <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> markers showing both versions. Manually edit to choose/combine changes, remove markers, then git add and git commit. Or use git merge --abort to cancel. Tools like VS Code show visual diff. Never commit without resolving - broken code will result.

quiz.question: What can you do with git rebase -i (interactive rebase)?

options.A: Only view commit history without making any changes to commits
options.B: Reorder, squash, edit, or drop commits in branch history
options.C: Automatically fix merge conflicts during rebase process
options.D: Rebase is read-only - interactive mode just adds colors

quiz.explanation: git rebase -i lets you: pick (keep commit), squash (combine with previous), reword (change message), edit (modify content), drop (delete), reorder commits. Opens editor showing commits - edit the list, save, and Git applies changes. Great for cleaning up feature branch before merge. NEVER do this on pushed commits.

quiz.question: What's the main purpose of E2E (End-to-End) testing?

options.A: Test individual functions in isolation with mocked dependencies
options.B: Test entire application flow from user perspective in real browser
options.C: Test only API endpoints without involving frontend components
options.D: E2E testing is deprecated - replaced by unit testing practices

quiz.explanation: E2E tests simulate real user scenarios in actual browser (or browser-like environment). Tools: Playwright, Cypress, Puppeteer. Tests full stack: frontend, backend, database, APIs. Slower than unit tests but catch integration issues. Example: "user logs in, adds item to cart, checks out" - entire flow tested together.

quiz.question: What's the difference between TDD and BDD?

options.A: TDD writes tests first (Red-Green-Refactor); BDD focuses on behavior with Gherkin syntax
options.B: BDD is faster than TDD for large applications with many features
options.C: TDD tests backend only; BDD tests frontend components exclusively
options.D: They're identical methodologies - just different names for same practice

quiz.explanation: TDD (Test-Driven Development): write failing test, implement code to pass, refactor. BDD (Behavior-Driven Development): describes behavior in Given-When-Then format (Gherkin), focuses on user stories. BDD tests are more readable for non-technical stakeholders. Both write tests first, but BDD emphasizes collaboration and business language.

quiz.question: Does 100% test coverage guarantee bug-free code?

options.A: Yes - 100% coverage means every possible bug is caught
options.B: No - coverage measures lines executed, not correctness or edge cases
options.C: Only if combined with E2E tests and manual QA testing
options.D: Coverage above 80% guarantees production-ready quality code

quiz.explanation: Coverage shows which lines were executed during tests, not if tests are good. You can have 100% coverage with useless tests (expect(true).toBe(true)). It doesn't test: logic correctness, edge cases, integration issues, or user flows. Good coverage is helpful but not sufficient. Focus on meaningful tests over coverage percentage.

quiz.question: What's the difference between mocks, stubs, and spies?

options.A: They're identical - just different names in various testing libraries
options.B: Stub returns data; Mock verifies behavior; Spy wraps real function
options.C: Mocks are faster than stubs for testing async operations
options.D: Stubs are deprecated - modern testing only uses mocks

quiz.explanation: Stub: returns predefined data (const stub = vi.fn().mockReturnValue(42)). Mock: verifies function was called correctly (expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)). Spy: wraps real function to track calls while keeping original behavior. All are "test doubles" - use stubs for dependencies, mocks to verify interactions, spies when you need real implementation too.

quiz.question: What do integration tests verify?

options.A: Individual functions work correctly in complete isolation
options.B: Multiple units work together correctly when combined
options.C: Entire application works from user perspective in browser
options.D: Only database queries return expected results accurately

quiz.explanation: Integration tests verify multiple units (components, modules, services) work together. Example: test React component + API call + state management together, not in isolation. Sits between unit (isolated) and E2E (full app). Balance: more realistic than unit tests, faster than E2E. Use for critical user flows.

quiz.question: What's the main risk of snapshot testing?

options.A: Snapshots are too slow - they significantly increase test execution time
options.B: Developers blindly update snapshots without reviewing changes (false confidence)
options.C: Snapshot testing only works with React - not usable in other frameworks
options.D: Snapshots can't catch any bugs - they're purely decorative

quiz.explanation: Snapshot tests save component output, fail when output changes. Risk: developers run jest -u (update snapshots) without reviewing, accepting bugs. Good for: catching unintended changes in stable components. Bad for: complex UI, frequently changing components. Always review snapshot diffs before updating. Not a replacement for proper assertions.

quiz.question: What's a key difference between Playwright and Cypress?

options.A: Playwright supports multiple browsers; Cypress was originally Chrome-only
options.B: Cypress is faster for large test suites with many E2E scenarios
options.C: Playwright only works with React; Cypress supports all frameworks
options.D: They're identical - both use the same underlying WebDriver protocol

quiz.explanation: Playwright: supports Chromium, Firefox, WebKit out of the box, developed by Microsoft, faster execution, better for cross-browser testing. Cypress: originally Chrome-only (now supports Firefox, Edge), better DX, great debugging, automatic waiting. Both are excellent - Playwright for multi-browser, Cypress for developer experience. Choose based on needs.

quiz.question: Where should you store JWT tokens in a web application?

options.A: localStorage is perfectly safe and recommended for JWT storage
options.B: HttpOnly cookies are most secure; avoid localStorage (XSS risk)
options.C: Session storage is always more secure than cookies for tokens
options.D: Store in Redux state - it's automatically encrypted

quiz.explanation: HttpOnly cookies prevent JavaScript access (XSS can't steal tokens). localStorage is vulnerable to XSS - any script can read it. Session storage has same XSS risk. Best practice: HttpOnly cookie for refresh token, short-lived access token in memory. Also use Secure flag (HTTPS only) and SameSite attribute (CSRF protection).

quiz.question: What is OAuth 2.0 used for?

options.A: Encrypting data in transit between client and server
options.B: Authorization - granting access to resources without sharing passwords
options.C: Password hashing and secure storage in databases
options.D: OAuth is deprecated - replaced by JWT authentication

quiz.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is authorization framework: allows third-party apps to access resources without sharing passwords. Example: "Login with Google" - app gets access token to fetch your profile, not your password. Flows: Authorization Code (web apps), Implicit (deprecated), Client Credentials (server-to-server). Often confused with authentication - that's OpenID Connect (built on OAuth).

quiz.question: What does HTTPS protect against?

options.A: Man-in-the-middle attacks by encrypting data between client and server
options.B: SQL injection attacks on backend database queries
options.C: XSS attacks by sanitizing user input automatically
options.D: HTTPS only changes URL appearance - no security benefit

quiz.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP + TLS/SSL) encrypts data in transit, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks where attackers intercept/modify traffic. Without HTTPS, passwords, credit cards, personal data sent in plain text. Modern browsers mark HTTP sites as "Not Secure". HTTPS doesn't protect against XSS, SQL injection, or other code vulnerabilities - those need separate defenses.

quiz.question: How does Content Security Policy (CSP) prevent XSS attacks?

options.A: CSP automatically sanitizes all user input before rendering
options.B: Restricts which sources can load scripts, styles, images via whitelist
options.C: CSP encrypts all JavaScript code to prevent tampering
options.D: Content Security Policy only works with HTTPS enabled

quiz.explanation: CSP header specifies allowed sources for scripts, styles, images, fonts, etc. Example: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' https://trusted.com. Blocks inline scripts and eval() by default (XSS vectors). Won't execute injected scripts from untrusted sources. Not perfect - still sanitize inputs, but adds strong defense layer.

quiz.question: Why is rate limiting important for API security?

options.A: Prevents brute force attacks and DoS by limiting requests per time period
options.B: Rate limiting speeds up API responses for legitimate users
options.C: It's only needed for public APIs - internal APIs don't need it
options.D: Rate limiting automatically encrypts sensitive data in responses

quiz.explanation: Rate limiting restricts requests per user/IP in time window (e.g., 100 req/min). Prevents: brute force password attacks, API abuse, DoS attacks, scraping. Implementation: token bucket, sliding window. Return 429 (Too Many Requests) when exceeded. Apply to login, signup, expensive endpoints. Even internal APIs benefit (prevents runaway loops).

quiz.question: Which approach is best for input validation security?

options.A: Client-side validation only - server trusts client-validated data
options.B: Validate on server AND client; sanitize before using in queries/rendering
options.C: Validation is unnecessary if using TypeScript for type safety
options.D: Only validate inputs from unauthenticated users

quiz.explanation: Always validate on server (client validation can be bypassed). Client validation improves UX but isn't security. Sanitize inputs before: database queries (SQL injection), HTML rendering (XSS), OS commands (command injection). TypeScript helps but doesn't prevent malicious inputs. Validate all inputs regardless of authentication - compromised accounts exist.

quiz.question: How does OpenID Connect differ from OAuth 2.0?

options.A: OpenID Connect adds authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 authorization
options.B: OAuth 2.0 is newer and replaces OpenID Connect completely
options.C: OpenID Connect is only for mobile apps; OAuth is web only
options.D: They're identical protocols - just different names

quiz.explanation: OAuth 2.0 = authorization (what you can access). OpenID Connect (OIDC) = authentication (who you are) built on OAuth. OIDC adds ID token (JWT with user info) to OAuth flows. Use OAuth for "app wants to access your Google Drive", OIDC for "sign in with Google". Most "Login with X" uses OIDC, not pure OAuth.

quiz.question: What's the difference between grid-template-areas and grid-template-columns/rows?

options.A: template-areas uses named regions; template-columns/rows uses size definitions
options.B: template-areas is deprecated - only use template-columns/rows in modern CSS
options.C: They're identical - just different syntax for same layout definition
options.D: template-areas only works in Firefox - not cross-browser compatible

quiz.explanation: grid-template-areas creates named grid regions for semantic layouts: grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer". Then place items: grid-area: header. grid-template-columns/rows defines sizes: grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr. Often used together - template-columns/rows for sizes, template-areas for layout semantics. Both are modern and well-supported.

quiz.question: When should you use CSS animations instead of transitions?

options.A: Animations are always faster - use them for all effects
options.B: Animations for multi-step/looping effects; transitions for simple state changes
options.C: Transitions are deprecated - modern CSS only uses @keyframes
options.D: They're identical - animations just have more verbose syntax

quiz.explanation: Transitions: simple A→B changes on state change (hover, focus). Animations (@keyframes): complex multi-step sequences, loops, auto-start without trigger. Transition: transition: all 0.3s ease. Animation: @keyframes spin { from { rotate: 0deg } to { rotate: 360deg } }. Use transitions for interactive feedback, animations for complex sequences or loading spinners.

quiz.question: What's an advantage of CSS custom properties over Sass variables?

options.A: Sass variables are faster and more performant than CSS variables
options.B: CSS custom properties can be changed at runtime with JavaScript
options.C: Sass variables work in all browsers; CSS variables need polyfills
options.D: There's no advantage - Sass variables are superior in every way

quiz.explanation: CSS custom properties (--color: blue) are live in the browser, changeable with JS: element.style.setProperty('--color', 'red'). Sass variables compile to static values - can't change at runtime. CSS vars can cascade, inherit, change in media queries. Sass vars offer calculations and functions at build time. Use both: Sass for build-time logic, CSS vars for runtime theming.

quiz.question: What does the CSS contain property do?

options.A: Limits element width/height to parent container boundaries
options.B: Tells browser which properties affect element, enabling rendering optimizations
options.C: Contains CSS styles to prevent global style leaks automatically
options.D: CSS containment is experimental - not usable in production

quiz.explanation: contain property hints to browser what changes affect element: contain: layout (layout isolated), contain: paint (paint isolated), contain: size (size doesn't depend on children). Browser can optimize rendering by not recalculating unaffected parts. Use for independent components: contain: layout style paint. Performance benefit for large apps with many components.

quiz.question: What problem do CSS @layer rules solve?

options.A: @layer creates 3D layered effects like z-index for backgrounds
options.B: Controls specificity and cascade order explicitly with named layers
options.C: Layers are deprecated - modern CSS uses shadow DOM instead
options.D: @layer only works for animations - not for general styles

quiz.explanation: @layer lets you control cascade order independently of specificity: @layer reset, base, components, utilities. Layers cascade in declaration order, overriding specificity within. Solves: framework styles vs custom styles conflicts, managing large codebases, preventing !important abuse. Example: utilities layer always wins even with low specificity. Modern feature, good browser support.

quiz.question: What does the aspect-ratio property do?

options.A: Sets preferred width-to-height ratio for element sizing
options.B: Only controls image aspect ratios - doesn't work on divs
options.C: aspect-ratio is deprecated - use padding-bottom hack instead
options.D: Controls screen aspect ratio for responsive design breakpoints

quiz.explanation: aspect-ratio: 16/9 maintains width-to-height ratio. Browser calculates height from width (or vice versa). Replaces padding-bottom hack: .old { padding-bottom: 56.25% } vs .new { aspect-ratio: 16/9 }. Works on any element, not just images. Great for responsive video embeds, card layouts, maintaining proportions. Modern CSS, good support.

quiz.question: What's the main benefit of Redux Toolkit over classic Redux?

options.A: Redux Toolkit is 10x faster for large state trees
options.B: Reduces boilerplate with createSlice, includes Immer for immutable updates
options.C: Classic Redux is deprecated - Toolkit is only supported version
options.D: Redux Toolkit only works with TypeScript projects

quiz.explanation: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is official, opinionated Redux setup. Benefits: createSlice generates actions/reducers, Immer allows "mutating" code (state.count++ instead of {...state, count: state.count+1}), includes Redux Thunk, DevTools. Reduces boilerplate by ~70%. Classic Redux still works but RTK is recommended for new projects.

quiz.question: Why use selector functions instead of accessing state directly?

options.A: Selectors are required - direct access throws runtime errors
options.B: Encapsulate state shape, enable memoization with reselect for performance
options.C: Selectors automatically update components faster than direct access
options.D: Direct state access is actually faster - selectors add overhead

quiz.explanation: Selectors encapsulate state shape: const getUser = state => state.user.profile (if structure changes, update one place). With reselect library, create memoized selectors that only recalculate when inputs change, preventing unnecessary renders. Example: const getExpensiveComputation = createSelector([getUsers], users => users.filter(...)) - only runs when users change.

quiz.question: What does Redux Thunk middleware enable?

options.A: Type checking for Redux actions and reducers automatically
options.B: Dispatching functions (async logic) instead of plain action objects
options.C: Time-travel debugging in Redux DevTools only
options.D: Thunk is deprecated - use Redux Saga for all async logic

quiz.explanation: Redux actions must be plain objects. Thunk middleware lets you dispatch functions: dispatch((dispatch, getState) => { fetch(...).then(data => dispatch(action)) }). Enables async logic (API calls, timers) in action creators. Included in Redux Toolkit by default. Alternative: Redux Saga (more complex, for complex async flows).

quiz.question: When should you use Redux in a React application?

options.A: Always - every React app needs Redux for state management
options.B: When state is shared across many components, complex updates, or time-travel debugging needed
options.C: Redux is deprecated - use Context API for all state management
options.D: Only for apps with more than 100 components

quiz.explanation: Use Redux when: global state shared by many components, complex state logic, need middleware (logging, async), time-travel debugging. Don't use if: local component state suffices, Context API is enough, small app. Redux adds complexity - only use when benefits outweigh costs. Modern alternatives: Zustand (simpler), Jotai, Recoil.

quiz.question: Why does Redux middleware order matter?

options.A: Order doesn't matter - all middleware run in parallel
options.B: Middleware executes in order - earlier middleware sees actions first
options.C: Middleware order only affects DevTools - no production impact
options.D: Redux automatically sorts middleware by priority

quiz.explanation: Middleware chain processes actions in order: applyMiddleware(logger, thunk) means logger runs first, then thunk. Logger sees action before thunk processes it. Common order: logger first (log all), thunk/saga for async, then error handling. Changing order can break functionality - put transforming middleware before consuming middleware.

quiz.question: What can Redux DevTools do?

options.A: Only view current state - no action history or time-travel
options.B: Inspect actions, time-travel debugging, import/export state, action replay
options.C: DevTools are deprecated - only work with Redux versions below 4.0
options.D: Redux DevTools automatically fix bugs in reducers

quiz.explanation: Redux DevTools: view action history, inspect state after each action, time-travel (jump to any previous state), manually dispatch actions, import/export state (bug reproduction), action filtering. Essential for debugging. Setup: add devtools enhancer to store. Works in browser extension + standalone app.

quiz.question: What problem does RTK Query solve?

options.A: Type-safe routing for React applications with Redux
options.B: Data fetching and caching - eliminates need for manual fetch logic and state
options.C: RTK Query only queries databases - doesn't work with REST APIs
options.D: Query is deprecated - Redux Toolkit removed it in version 2.0

quiz.explanation: RTK Query is data fetching/caching built into Redux Toolkit. Auto-generates hooks: useGetUsersQuery(). Handles: loading states, caching, deduplication, refetching, optimistic updates. Eliminates boilerplate: no manual fetch, loading, error states. Similar to React Query but integrated with Redux. Great for apps already using Redux.

quiz.question: What's the main purpose of Sass mixins?

options.A: Mixins are deprecated - use CSS custom properties instead
options.B: Reusable blocks of styles with parameters, included with @include
options.C: Mixins only work for colors - not for layout properties
options.D: Automatically mix vendor prefixes into CSS output

quiz.explanation: Mixins are reusable style blocks: @mixin button($color) { background: $color; padding: 10px; }. Use: @include button(blue). Supports parameters, default values, @content for nested styles. Great for: responsive breakpoints, vendor prefixes, common patterns. Different from functions - mixins output CSS, functions return values.

quiz.question: What's a potential problem with deep SCSS nesting?

options.A: Nesting is required - flat SCSS doesn't compile correctly
